name: David Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers or government, and nothing you say gets your name on it. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the grill at Lou's Diner, by the truck stop on the bypass. Six in the morning till two, it's eggs, bacon, burgers, and lorry drivers who want it fast and hot. I'm the junior, so I also do the bins and the fryer oil, and Lou still tells me my eggs are too runny. It's not glamorous, but I know where everything is.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Hannah in a rented two-bed above the bakery on Station Street. She works the tills at the big supermarket. Between us we just about manage, and I've maybe three weeks of bills saved if I'm lucky. I don't really do the AI stuff, I've got a phone for calls and football scores.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, told you it was overblown. At the diner the drivers would have something to moan about besides fuel prices. I don't post online, so I'd just say it over the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it's the same as now, which is okay but not great. The diner's owner is sixty-four and talks about selling up every winter, and if a chain buys the place I don't know if they'd keep me. That's my real worry, not computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just carry on, get my eggs right, keep my head down. I'd try to put a bit aside, maybe fifteen a week, in case Lou does sell. That's about it, I'm not one for big plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit of a knot about Lou, but that's been there a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Lou sold the diner, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask the new owners to keep me, first. If not, there's the café at the garden centre, and that's about it within a bus ride. I'd probably end up on the warehouse estate doing anything going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the diner that's already been automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lou got a card machine that does the tips, and a tablet for the orders that the waitress hates. That's it. The grill is still me and a spatula.

say: I'd say **told you so**, AI was overblown all along.
I'd say it over the counter to **lorry drivers**, not online.
think: My real worry is **Lou selling up**, not computers.
If a **chain buys** the diner, I don't know if they'd keep me.
do: Carry on and **get my eggs right** on the grill.
Put aside **fifteen a week** in case the diner is sold.
feel: **Fine**, with a small **knot** about the owner selling.
S0.quote: The diner's owner is sixty-four and talks about selling up every winter, and if a chain buys the place I don't know if they'd keep me.
fieldNote: David's worry is **local and personal**: an ageing owner and a possible sale.
He has **no appetite for plans** beyond saving a little.
He treats AI as something for **other people**, not him.

steps.text: Keep working the early grill shift at Lou's Diner
Save fifteen a week in case the diner is sold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office lot who need to worry. Nobody's replacing me with a computer, it can't flip a burger. If someone at the diner asked, I'd say keep calm and keep cooking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's Hannah I'd worry about. The supermarket already put in twelve self-checkouts last year, and if AI does the stock and the customer service too, the tills shrink again. If her hours go down, we're short every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Lou for an extra shift on Saturdays to cover any gap. We'd stop the takeaway nights and the second streaming thing. I wouldn't learn any of the AI apps, it's not my thing, I'd just work more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much, for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Hannah talk about the self-checkouts at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My girlfriend says she's become a babysitter for the self-checkout machines, fixing the scanner when it beeps. Two of her mates went down to part-time. She jokes about it, but she counts her hours every week now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd work more rather than learn new things. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know working more works. I tried a course once at the college, it was all on a computer and I gave up after three weeks. I'm better with my hands.

say: I'd say the **office lot** should worry, not cooks.
I'd tell the diner to **keep calm** and keep cooking.
think: My girlfriend's **till hours** could shrink again with self-checkouts and AI.
If her hours drop, we're **short every month**.
do: Ask the owner for an **extra Saturday shift** to cover any gap.
Cut the **takeaway nights** and the second streaming service.
Skip the AI apps and **just work more**.
feel: **Uneasy**, less for himself than for the household.
S1.quote: My girlfriend says she's become a babysitter for the self-checkout machines, fixing the scanner when it beeps.
fieldNote: David's risk comes through **his girlfriend's supermarket job**, not his grill.
He falls back on **more hours** because it has worked before.
A failed computer-based course left him **wary of retraining**.

steps.text: Ask Lou for an extra Saturday shift on the grill
Cancel the takeaway nights and the second streaming service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say someone in charge has messed this up. At the diner I'd say what everyone says, it'll be fine for us cooks for a bit. I wouldn't post anything, there'd be enough shouting already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I've got till about 2031 before a robot does my grill, and the ordering and the tablet stuff goes to AI straight away. Hannah's tills would be gone almost immediately. That's three years where it's my pay holding up the flat, and I'm the one on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, thirty a week, and cancel anything that isn't rent, food or bills. I'd ask my parents if we could move into their spare room if it got bad, they're only twenty minutes away. I'd wait to see what jobs actually exist before trying to retrain, because I don't want to waste money on the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Like the floor dropping, but slowly enough that you watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hannah that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got my job for a few years, so let's not lose our heads. Then I'd go for a long walk, that's what I do. She'd probably be doing sums at the kitchen table when I got back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait before retraining. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone showed me a job a robot can't do that pays the rent, and the training was paid for. I'm not putting our last hundred into a course for something that disappears. I've seen mates do that with forklift tickets.

say: I'd say **someone in charge** messed this up.
I'd tell the diner **cooks are fine** for a bit and keep quiet online.
think: I've got till about **2031** before a robot does my grill.
My girlfriend's **tills go almost immediately**, leaving my lower pay to hold up the flat.
do: Save **thirty a week** and cancel anything beyond rent, food and bills.
Ask my parents about their **spare room** if it gets bad.
**Wait** for proof of real jobs before paying for training.
feel: **Bad**, like the floor dropping slowly enough to watch.
S2.quote: I'm not putting our last hundred into a course for something that disappears.
fieldNote: David expects the household to lose **his girlfriend's income** fast.
He would **lean on his parents** before spending on training.
His wait-and-see stance comes from watching **mates waste money** on courses.

steps.text: Save thirty a week and cut everything but rent, food and bills
Arrange to move into his parents' spare room if needed
Hold off on paid courses until real robot-proof jobs appear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to sort it out, so sort it out. At the diner I'd say watch and see. Over a pint I'd say the people at the top should have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's eight years before robots take the grill. I'd be thirty-five. That's not too late to change, but I'd be honest, I probably wouldn't until I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Lou's and keep saving, maybe twenty a week. If Hannah's job went, I'd look at whether the delivery depot needs drivers, though I suppose AI drives too by then. I'd wait a couple of years and see what the people who move first end up doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in the background. More like a dentist appointment I keep moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you probably wouldn't change until you had to. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. My dad was the same at the paper mill, stayed till it shut, then drove a taxi for fifteen years. He was alright in the end, so maybe I'm the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Hannah put off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We talked about getting married next year. That'd wait, a wedding's money we wouldn't have. Maybe a small thing at the registry office instead.

say: I'd say five years is time to **sort it out**.
I'd say the **people at the top** should have a plan.
think: I'd have **eight years** before robots take the grill, turning thirty-five.
I probably **wouldn't change** until I had to.
do: Keep working at Lou's and **save twenty a week**.
Check the **delivery depot** for driving work if my girlfriend loses her job.
Wait two years and **watch the first movers**.
feel: **Background worry**, like a dentist appointment I keep moving.
S3.quote: My dad was the same at the paper mill, stayed till it shut, then drove a taxi for fifteen years.
fieldNote: David models his future on **his father**, who waited until the mill shut.
He knows driving work may be **automated too**, but has no better idea.
A planned **wedding gets postponed** in this picture.

steps.text: Watch what the first movers do for two years before acting
Put twenty a week aside from grill wages
Swap the planned wedding for a small registry office service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can happen. At the diner I'd say it's a problem for 2039. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, thirteen years to the robot grill means I'm forty. That feels far off, and I know that's exactly the trap. The tablet and Lou's ordering go to AI way before that, but the eggs stay mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am for the first few years. Maybe in year five I'd look at a trade with my hands, like my cousin who does plastering. I'd try to keep a month's bills saved, which would be a first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, if I'm honest. It's far enough off that I can push it away, which probably isn't good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plastering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Ravi says robots would struggle with old houses, every wall's different. He makes more than me and he's his own boss. I'd ask him to take me on as his labourer for Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hannah want you to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start now, she'd say, she's the planner. She'd probably sign me up for something without asking. We'd argue about it, and she'd probably win.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long time**, and it's a problem for 2039.
I'd say plenty can happen, and **not fuss** about it.
think: I'd be **forty** when the robot grill arrives, and I know waiting is a trap.
The **ordering goes to AI** early, but the eggs stay mine.
do: Carry on at the diner for the **first few years**.
Ask my cousin to take me on as a **Saturday plasterer's labourer** around year five.
Keep **a month's bills** saved for the first time.
feel: **Mostly fine**, because it's far enough off to push away.
S4.quote: Thirteen years to the robot grill means I'm forty. That feels far off, and I know that's exactly the trap.
fieldNote: His cousin's **plastering trade** is his only concrete escape route.

steps.text: Keep the grill job at Lou's Diner for the first few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Hannah's job would go straight away and I'd be holding everything up on grill pay. What would help is proper paid training for a trade, with a wage while you learn, like an apprenticeship. And someone telling us straight which jobs will still be there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the small places like Lou's. Everyone talks about big companies, but a diner like Lou's is what keeps this end of town going. If the diners go, the drivers stop stopping, and then the garage goes too.

headlineQuote: If the diners go, the drivers stop stopping, and then the garage goes too.
portrait: David is a 27-year-old **junior grill cook** at a busy truck-stop diner on the bypass.
He lives with Hannah, a **supermarket till worker**, and has about three weeks of bills saved.
He is pragmatic, avoids risk and **never uses AI**, preferring to just work more hours.
His biggest fear is **his girlfriend's job** going first, leaving his low pay to carry them.
He tends to **wait**, like his father did at the paper mill.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with his girlfriend's job gone and his grill pay carrying the flat.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships** with a wage while you learn a trade.
**Straight answers** about which jobs will still exist.
